Chapter seven: The Struggle to Remember—Preserving Covert’s Story.
You know how time just has this way of softening memories? The longer the years went by, the more those sharp details from Covert’s early days started to blur. New generations grew up with only bits and pieces—maybe a story shared around the dinner table, a name weathered into a gravestone, or an old photo hidden in the back of a drawer. The world outside kept shifting, and with it, the sense of urgency behind Covert’s experiment seemed to fade.
But here’s the thing—not everyone was willing to let those memories just disappear. There was an older woman in town, now a grandmother, who decided she wasn’t going to let the story slip away. She made it her mission to gather up the memories of those who’d come before. Picture her, spending her afternoons listening to neighbors, jotting down notes as they reminisced about harsh winters, barn raisings, and those quiet moments of defiance that shaped the town. She collected old letters, church records, even school rosters—slowly stitching together a patchwork of voices and moments.
One day, she invited a group of children into her kitchen. Over cookies and lemonade, she started sharing the stories of Covert’s founders—how they’d welcomed strangers, stood up to outsiders, and built something truly different. The kids sat there, wide-eyed, as she described a time when the world seemed determined to keep people apart, and how this little town dared to choose another route.
Inspired by these stories, a local teacher decided to bring them right into the classroom. She encouraged her students to talk with their elders, to walk the same old roads and imagine what life was like back then. Sure, some of the kids grumbled at first, but before long, the drama and hope woven through the past really pulled them in.
Most folks don’t realize just how easily history can be lost—not because someone’s trying to erase it, but simply through neglect. In Covert, remembering became an act of resistance. It was their way of honoring the courage of those who came before. It’s a powerful reminder that the past isn’t just a list of names and dates—it’s a living inheritance, a collection of values and choices that still mean something right now.
When the town came together for its anniversaries, the story of Covert was told and retold. Sometimes it sounded polished and proud, other times it felt raw and uncertain. But the message was always the same: ordinary people, working side by side, can build something extraordinary.
So, the act of remembering? It became a way to keep hope alive—to remind every new generation that the work of inclusion is never truly finished.
